steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on sample-efficient factored embeddings of tensor fields. Motivate tensor sketching for huge data collections, explain the limits of randomized sketching and existing sampling schemes, introduce our Progressive Sketching method (P-SCT) with Thompson sampling, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Huge data tensors and the case for compact tensor sketches
- Randomized sketching background: SketchySVD, SketchyCoreSVD, our R-SCT / R-SCTT
- Limitations of random sampling (R-SCT)
- Prior sampling-based Tucker decompositions and their problems
- Our method: Progressive Sketching (P-SCT)
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Huge data tensors
  - tensors of order 2+ routinely generated; collections huge and growing
  - e.g. North American Regional Reanalysis (NARR): 70 climate variables every 3 hours, 1979 to present, 29.4 Terabytes
  - tensor fields: each data location holds important info
  - direct access increasingly prohibitive
  - approximate low rank, low memory (compact) tensor sketches: space/time efficient; querying + post-processing done on sketches with high accuracy
- Randomized sketching
  - popular for low rank approximation of very large matrices and tensors
  - faster than SVD, similar accuracy
  - SketchyCoreSVD: sketches only from sub-sampled + projected columns and rows -> faster, less memory
  - advances SketchySVD by exploiting redundancy (incoherence)
  - SketchySVD extended to low-rank Tucker decomposition of tensors
  - we derive Randomized SketchyCoreTucker (R-SCT) + randomized sketchy Tensor Train (R-SCTT) in Appendix
- Limitations of R-SCT
  - mathematically proven, computationally advantageous, but inherent variance (random sampling, user-defined sub-sampling ratios)
  - random subsets -> suboptimal/inefficient for sparse structured data
  - info concentrated in small regions: tissue patterns in medical scans; storms/droughts in satellite climate data
  - irrelevant/duplicate samples: memory without accuracy gain
  - also needs optimal sampling ratios given compute resources
- Prior sampling-based Tucker
  - mostly sample columns of matrix unfoldings
  - prior multi-variate Gaussian distribution (theoretically fastest) but suboptimal over sampling sequence; inefficient total sample size
  - leverage scores for informativeness distribution: more info, but problematic for higher order, very large tensors
- Progressive Sketching
  - progressively samples row vectors of matrix unfolding (order K-1 slice of order K tensor) from actively updated informativeness distribution
  - learns optimal sub-sampling sequence policy for factored sketches; near-optimal, sample efficient -> best low rank, low memory approx with smallest sample use
  - P-SCT: more accurate than R-SCT with same amount of data subsets
  - applies to any randomized sketching based ML algorithm; learned sequential decision making agents
  - Bayesian Thompson sampling first; extendable to local uncertainty for contextual bandits
  - deep RL (Soft Actor-Critic, Soft Q-learning with mutual information regularization) also usable
  - validated on large static and time-varying datasets vs randomized decomposition methods
- Contributions
  - P-SCT for tensor fields; learns optimal Thompson sampling policy using Dirichlet distribution
  - learned compact, effective latent space embeddings; factored tensor usable for many large data-driven tasks
  - complexity analysis + empirical comparisons; much fewer data fiber samples than R-SCT and full-scan factorizations

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Data tensors of order 2 and higher are generated routinely, and these data collections are getting increasingly huge and keep growing. For example, the North American Regional Reanalysis (NARR) has collected 70 climate variables every 3 hours from 1979 to the present, and its total size is currently 29.4 Terabytes. These data tensors are tensor fields where each location of data contains important information. Accessing such large collections of data tensors directly to get information is becoming more and more prohibitive. Generating approximate low rank and low memory (compact) tensor sketches is a space and time efficient alternative, because all of the information querying and post-processing is done on the sketches with high accuracy.

Randomized sketching algorithms are a popular way to produce a low rank approximation of very large matrices and tensors. These algorithms are faster than the singular value decomposition (SVD) and their approximation accuracy is similar to the SVD. Recently, SketchyCoreSVD was proposed, which speeds up the computation more and reduces the memory requirement by building random sketches only from columns and rows that are sub-sampled and projected. It improves on SketchySVD by exploiting redundancy in the data matrix, which can be characterized by incoherence. SketchySVD had been extended to compute the approximate low-rank Tucker decomposition of tensors. With similar ideas as in SketchyCoreSVD, we derive a Randomized SketchyCoreTucker (R-SCT) decomposition of tensor fields, and in the Appendix a randomized sketchy version of the Tensor Train decomposition (R-SCTT).

R-SCT is mathematically proven and has computational advantages, but its performance has an inherent variance because of the random sampling protocol and the sub-sampling ratios that the user defines. R-SCT samples data subsets randomly from the original data tensor, so it can be suboptimal and inefficient for data that is sparse and structured. In a lot of modern scientific data the meaningful information is often concentrated in small regions, for example specific patterns of tissue in medical scans, or extreme climate events like storms or droughts in satellite climate data. If we sample irrelevant or duplicate subsets we use memory unnecessarily and the accuracy does not improve. Also, the performance of the method can be affected by the additional requirement of optimal sampling ratios given the computational resources that are available.

- prior sampling-based Tucker decompositions: mostly sample columns of matrix unfoldings; prior multi-variate Gaussian (theoretically fastest) but suboptimal over sampling sequence, inefficient total sample size; leverage scores -> informativeness distribution, more info but problematic for higher order / very large tensors
- Progressive Sketching: progressively sample row vectors of matrix unfolding (order K-1 slice of order K tensor) from actively updated informativeness distribution; learn optimal sub-sampling sequence policy; sample efficient, near-optimal -> best low rank, low memory approx with smallest sample use
- P-SCT more accurate than R-SCT with same data subsets; applicable to any randomized sketching ML algorithm, as learned sequential decision making agents; Bayesian Thompson sampling first, extendable to local uncertainty for contextual bandits; deep RL (Soft Actor-Critic, Soft Q-learning w/ mutual information regularization) also possible; validated on large static + time-varying datasets vs randomized decomposition methods
- contributions: P-SCT with Thompson sampling policy via Dirichlet distribution; compact, effective latent space embeddings for large data-driven tasks; complexity analysis + experiments, far fewer data fiber samples than R-SCT and full-scan factorizations

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Data tensors of order 2 and higher are generated routinely, and these data collections are getting increasingly huge and keep growing. For example, the North American Regional Reanalysis (NARR) has collected 70 climate variables every 3 hours from 1979 to the present, and its total size is currently 29.4 Terabytes. These data tensors are tensor fields where each location of data contains important information. Accessing such large collections of data tensors directly to get information is becoming more and more prohibitive. Generating approximate low rank and low memory (compact) tensor sketches is a space and time efficient alternative, because all of the information querying and post-processing is done on the sketches with high accuracy.

Randomized sketching algorithms are a popular way to produce a low rank approximation of very large matrices and tensors. These algorithms are faster than the singular value decomposition (SVD) and their approximation accuracy is similar to the SVD. Recently, SketchyCoreSVD was proposed, which speeds up the computation more and reduces the memory requirement by building random sketches only from columns and rows that are sub-sampled and projected. It improves on SketchySVD by exploiting redundancy in the data matrix, which can be characterized by incoherence. SketchySVD had been extended to compute the approximate low-rank Tucker decomposition of tensors. With similar ideas as in SketchyCoreSVD, we derive a Randomized SketchyCoreTucker (R-SCT) decomposition of tensor fields, and in the Appendix a randomized sketchy version of the Tensor Train decomposition (R-SCTT).

R-SCT is mathematically proven and has computational advantages, but its performance has an inherent variance because of the random sampling protocol and the sub-sampling ratios that the user defines. R-SCT samples data subsets randomly from the original data tensor, so it can be suboptimal and inefficient for data that is sparse and structured. In a lot of modern scientific data the meaningful information is often concentrated in small regions, for example specific patterns of tissue in medical scans, or extreme climate events like storms or droughts in satellite climate data. If we sample irrelevant or duplicate subsets we use memory unnecessarily and the accuracy does not improve. Also, the performance of the method can be affected by the additional requirement of optimal sampling ratios given the computational resources that are available.

Randomized sampling based Tucker decompositions have been studied before, but most of the algorithms sample columns of matrix unfoldings. Most randomized sampling based algorithms also use a prior multi-variate Gaussian distribution, because these are theoretically the fastest. But they are suboptimal over the sampling sequence and the total sample size they need is inefficient. Other algorithms use measures like leverage scores to infer an informativeness distribution. These algorithms use more information, but they have problems for higher order and very large data tensors.

To overcome some of these challenges, we present a new method that we call Progressive Sketching. It progressively samples row vectors of the matrix unfolding of the input tensor (i.e., an order K-1 tensor slice of the order K input tensor) from an informativeness distribution that is actively updated. This way we actively learn an optimal sub-sampling sequence policy for factored tensor sketches. When we learn a sub-sampling policy that is sample efficient and near-optimal, we can easily give the best low rank and low memory approximation of the tensor fields while using the smallest number of samples.

Progressive SketchyCoreTucker sketching (P-SCT) gives low rank approximations that are more accurate than R-SCT using the same amount of input data subsets. So P-SCT gives a factored tensor sketch that is sample efficient. Our progressive learned factored sketching can be applied to any machine learning algorithm based on randomized sketching, and it can be formulated as learned sequential decision making agents. In this paper we use a Bayesian Thompson sampling framework first. This Thompson sampling framework can be extended to a local uncertainty framework for contextual bandits. Deep reinforcement learning algorithms like Soft Actor-Critic or Soft Q-learning with mutual information regularization can also be used for progressive sketching based on the algorithm in this paper. We validate how P-SCT performs on different large static and time-varying datasets and compare it quantitatively to a class of randomized decomposition methods.

The main contributions of this paper are the following:

- A new progressive sketching method (P-SCT) for tensor fields, which further optimizes the performance of randomized sketching by also learning an optimal Thompson sampling policy for tensor sketching, using Dirichlet distribution;

- P-SCT is a learned way to generate compact (low memory) and effective latent space embeddings. The factored tensor can be used universally for several very large data driven tasks;

- With complexity analysis and empirical comparisons we show how progressive sketching can optimize randomized sketching further and produce accurate low rank approximations. P-SCT also uses a much smaller number of data fiber samples than R-SCT and other full-scan tensor factorization algorithms.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Data tensors of orders 2 and greater are routinely being generated, and these data collections are increasingly huge and growing. For instance, the North American Regional Reanalysis (NARR) has been collecting 70 climate variables every 3 hours from 1979 to the present, and it is currently at a total size of 29.4 Terabytes [1]. These data tensors are tensor fields in which each location of data contains important information. Directly accessing such large data tensor collections for information has become increasingly prohibitive. Generating approximate low rank and low memory (compact) tensor sketches provides a space and time efficient alternative, as all information querying and post-processing is performed on the sketches with high accuracy.

Randomized sketching algorithms have been a popular approach for producing low rank approximations of very large matrices and tensors [2,3,4,5,6,7]. These algorithms are faster than the singular value decomposition (SVD) while keeping an approximation accuracy similar to the SVD. Recently, SketchyCoreSVD was proposed to further speed up the computation and reduce the memory requirement by building random sketches only from sub-sampled and projected columns and rows [8]. It advances SketchySVD [9] by exploiting redundancy in the data matrix, which can be characterized by incoherence. SketchySVD had also been extended to compute the approximate low-rank Tucker decomposition of tensors [10]. Using similar ideas as in SketchyCoreSVD [8], we derive a Randomized SketchyCoreTucker (R-SCT) decomposition of tensor fields, and a randomized sketchy version of the Tensor Train decomposition (R-SCTT) in the Appendix.

R-SCT is mathematically proven and computationally advantageous, but its performance has an inherent variance due to the random sampling protocol and the user-defined sub-sampling ratios. Since R-SCT randomly samples data subsets from the original data tensor, it can be suboptimal and inefficient for sparse structured data. In many modern scientific data, meaningful information is often concentrated in small regions, e.g., specific patterns of tissue in medical scans or extreme climate events such as storms or droughts in satellite climate data. Sampling irrelevant or duplicate subsets leads to unnecessary memory consumption without improving accuracy. Moreover, the performance of the method can be impacted by the additional requirement of optimal sampling ratios given the available computational resources.

While randomized sampling based Tucker decompositions have been studied in the past, most algorithms sample columns of matrix unfoldings [11]. Most randomized sampling based algorithms also utilize a prior multi-variate Gaussian distribution [12], since these are theoretically the fastest; however, they are suboptimal over the sampling sequence, and the total required sample size is inefficient. Other algorithms utilize measures such as leverage scores [13,14,15] to infer an informativeness distribution. These algorithms use more information, but they are problematic for higher order and very large data tensors.

To overcome several of these challenges, we present a new method called Progressive Sketching, which progressively samples row vectors of the matrix unfolding of the input tensor (i.e., an order K-1 tensor slice of the order K input tensor) from an actively updated informativeness distribution. In this way, we actively learn an optimal sub-sampling sequence policy for factored tensor sketches. By learning a sample efficient and near-optimal sub-sampling policy, one can then easily provide the best low rank and low memory approximation of the tensor fields with the smallest sample use.

Progressive SketchyCoreTucker sketching (P-SCT) produces more accurate low rank approximations than R-SCT using the same amount of input data subsets; in other words, P-SCT yields a sample efficient factored tensor sketch. Our progressive learned factored sketching can be applied to any randomized sketching based machine learning algorithm and formulated as learned sequential decision making agents. In this paper, we first use a Bayesian Thompson sampling framework, which can be extended to a local uncertainty framework for contextual bandits [16]. Deep reinforcement learning algorithms, such as Soft Actor-Critic [17,18,19] or Soft Q-learning with mutual information regularization [20], can also be used for progressive sketching based on the algorithm introduced here. We validate the performance of P-SCT on various large static and time-varying datasets, quantitatively comparing it to a class of randomized decomposition methods.

Overall, the main contributions of this paper are the following:

- A new progressive sketching method (P-SCT) applicable to tensor fields, which further optimizes the performance of randomized sketching by additionally learning an optimal Thompson sampling policy for tensor sketching, using Dirichlet distribution;

- P-SCT is a learned generation of compact (low memory) and effective latent space embeddings, and the factored tensor can be universally utilized for several very large data driven tasks;

- Through complexity analysis and empirical comparisons, we show how progressive sketching can further optimize randomized sketching to produce accurate low rank approximations. Moreover, P-SCT utilizes a much smaller number of data fiber samples than R-SCT and other full-scan tensor factorization algorithms.
